body.heading: Every question starts somewhere
paragraphs: Questions are how we learn anything — and almost every question in English begins with one of six small words. Each one asks for a different kind of answer. Knowing which one you need is the first skill of every detective, scientist and reporter.

body.heading: Who and what
paragraphs: Who — asks about a person. Who left this muddy footprint?
What — asks about a thing, an action or an idea. What is inside the box?

body.heading: Where and when
paragraphs: Where — asks about a place. Where does the river begin?
When — asks about a time. When does the library open?

body.heading: Why and how
paragraphs: Why — asks for a reason. Why is the sky blue? (Why is the most powerful question word of all — it is the one scientists live on.)
How — asks about the way something happens, or how much or how many. How does a bee find its way home?

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Pick a mystery — a squeaky door, a missing sock — and write one question with each of the six words. Which question would you investigate first?
2. Interview a family member using only W questions. You may not ask anything that can be answered with plain yes or no!

takeaway: Who asks for a person, what for a thing, where for a place, when for a time, why for a reason, and how for a method — six keys that open every question.
materials: Just you and this page — no materials needed
supervision: A grown-up nearby is recommended for younger readers; the think-and-talk questions work well read aloud together.
